questions.title: Build a home loan amortisation schedule
questions.scenario: Rohan Mehta in the retail loans team gets daily calls from home loan customers asking how much of each EMI goes to interest. He wants the full month-by-month schedule generated in SQL instead of a spreadsheet, with the last EMI adjusted so the balance closes at exactly zero.
questions.schema:
LOAN(loan_id NUMBER, principal NUMBER(14,2), annual_rate NUMBER(5,2), tenure_months NUMBER, emi NUMBER(12,2), first_due DATE)
-- annual_rate like 8.75 (percent per year); emi is the fixed monthly instalment in INR
-- first_due is the first EMI date, no time part
questions.task: For one loan (:loan_id) list month_no, due_date, opening balance, interest, principal part, closing balance and amount due, ending with a zero closing balance.
questions.hint: Use recursive subquery factoring that carries the opening balance forward one month at a time, and compute due dates from first_due, not from the previous due date.
questions.solution:
WITH sched (loan_id, month_no, due_date, opening, annual_rate, emi, tenure_months, first_due) AS (
  SELECT loan_id, 1, first_due, principal, annual_rate, emi, tenure_months, first_due
  FROM   loan
  WHERE  loan_id = :loan_id
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.loan_id, s.month_no + 1,
         ADD_MONTHS(s.first_due, s.month_no),
         s.opening - (s.emi - ROUND(s.opening * s.annual_rate / 1200, 2)),
         s.annual_rate, s.emi, s.tenure_months, s.first_due
  FROM   sched s
  WHERE  s.month_no < s.tenure_months
)
SELECT month_no, due_date, opening,
       ROUND(opening * annual_rate / 1200, 2) AS interest,
       CASE WHEN month_no = tenure_months THEN opening
            ELSE emi - ROUND(opening * annual_rate / 1200, 2) END AS principal_part,
       CASE WHEN month_no = tenure_months THEN 0
            ELSE opening - (emi - ROUND(opening * annual_rate / 1200, 2)) END AS closing,
       CASE WHEN month_no = tenure_months
            THEN opening + ROUND(opening * annual_rate / 1200, 2)
            ELSE emi END AS amount_due
FROM   sched
ORDER  BY month_no;
questions.why: The anchor row is month 1 with the full principal; each recursive step subtracts that month's principal part (EMI minus interest at rate/1200) to get the next opening balance. The last month pays whatever is left plus its interest, so rounding differences do not leave a few rupees outstanding. Due dates use ADD_MONTHS from first_due so a 31st does not drift to the 28th forever after February.
questions.tip: Recursive WITH needs a column list, an anchor, a recursive member that references the CTE once, and a stop condition; I keep the stop condition on a counter so it can never loop.
questions.simple: A loan schedule is like a staircase. Each month you start with what you owe, pay some interest and some of the loan, and what is left becomes next month's starting point. A recursive WITH builds one step, then uses it to build the next step, until the loan is paid off.
questions.remember: Recursive WITH = build the next row from the row before.

questions.title: Sector-wise GNPA for regulatory return
questions.scenario: Ananya Iyer prepares the quarterly sector-wise advances return for RBI. She needs outstanding and gross NPA by region and sector, sector totals across all regions, and a grand total, but the format has no region subtotal rows. Some legacy loans have no sector and must show as 'Unclassified', not be confused with a total row.
questions.schema:
ADVANCES(loan_id NUMBER, region VARCHAR2(20), sector VARCHAR2(30), npa_flag CHAR(1), outstanding NUMBER(16,2), asof_date DATE)
-- sector like 'Agriculture','MSME','Retail' or NULL for legacy loans
-- npa_flag 'Y' or 'N'; asof_date is the snapshot date with no time part
questions.task: For the 31-Mar-2026 snapshot return row_type, region, sector, total outstanding, NPA outstanding and GNPA % for (region, sector), (sector) and grand total only.
questions.hint: GROUPING SETS lets you list exactly the groupings you want, and GROUPING() tells a real NULL apart from a subtotal NULL.
questions.solution:
SELECT CASE GROUPING_ID(region, sector)
         WHEN 0 THEN 'Region x Sector'
         WHEN 2 THEN 'Sector total'
         WHEN 3 THEN 'Grand total'
       END AS row_type,
       CASE WHEN GROUPING(region) = 1 THEN 'ALL' ELSE NVL(region, 'Unknown') END AS region,
       CASE WHEN GROUPING(sector) = 1 THEN 'ALL' ELSE NVL(sector, 'Unclassified') END AS sector,
       SUM(outstanding) AS total_os,
       SUM(CASE WHEN npa_flag = 'Y' THEN outstanding ELSE 0 END) AS npa_os,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(CASE WHEN npa_flag = 'Y' THEN outstanding ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(SUM(outstanding), 0), 2) AS gnpa_pct
FROM   advances
WHERE  asof_date = DATE '2026-03-31'
GROUP  BY GROUPING SETS ((region, sector), (sector), ())
ORDER  BY GROUPING_ID(region, sector), sector, region;
questions.why: ROLLUP(region, sector) would produce region subtotals and no sector totals, so GROUPING SETS is the precise tool. GROUPING_ID builds a bit pattern (region = 2, sector = 1), giving 0 for detail, 2 for sector totals and 3 for the grand total. Checking GROUPING() before NVL means a legacy loan with NULL sector shows 'Unclassified' while the subtotal row shows 'ALL'.
questions.tip: ROLLUP and CUBE are shortcuts for fixed sets of groupings; when a report format needs a specific mix I write GROUPING SETS and label rows with GROUPING_ID.
questions.simple: The report needs some lines by sector and region, some totals by sector, and one grand total, but not every possible mix. GROUPING SETS lets you list exactly which totals you want, like picking only the dishes you want from a menu instead of the full buffet.
questions.remember: GROUPING SETS = choose exactly which totals you want.

questions.title: Optional-filter AML alert search
questions.scenario: Vikram Rao's AML operations screen lets analysts filter open alerts by branch, minimum amount and from-date, any of which can be blank. The current code concatenates the typed values into the SQL string, which the information security audit flagged as SQL injection risk, and the DBA says it floods the shared pool with one-off statements.
questions.schema:
AML_ALERT(alert_id NUMBER, cust_id NUMBER, branch_code VARCHAR2(10), alert_amt NUMBER(14,2), alert_dt DATE, status VARCHAR2(10))
-- status 'OPEN' or 'CLOSED'; alert_amt in INR
questions.task: Write a function get_alerts(p_branch, p_min_amt, p_from_dt) that returns a SYS_REFCURSOR of open alerts, applying only the filters that are not NULL, using bind variables only.
questions.hint: Keep the number of binds fixed by adding a harmless '(1 = 1 OR :x IS NULL)' when a filter is not supplied, then OPEN ... FOR ... USING.
questions.why: User values never become part of the SQL text, they are passed through USING, so nothing typed can change the statement and injection is impossible. There are at most 8 distinct SQL texts, so Oracle parses each once and reuses its plan instead of hard-parsing (building a fresh plan, which is CPU-heavy) for every search. Each text only has the predicates that apply, so the optimizer can use an index on branch_code when that filter is given.
questions.tip: With dynamic SQL I bind values and only concatenate structure I control; the '1 = 1 OR :x IS NULL' trick keeps the USING list fixed while each filter combination still gets its own good plan.
questions.simple: A search screen where the user fills only some boxes. You build the SQL with only the filters they filled. But you never paste what they typed into the SQL; you pass it separately, like putting a letter in an envelope instead of writing on the outside. That keeps it safe from hackers and fast.
questions.remember: Build the shape, pass the values separately with binds.

questions.title: Carry forward USD/INR on holidays
questions.scenario: Sneha Kulkarni in treasury revalues foreign currency positions every calendar day, but reference rates are only published on business days. For weekends and holidays she must use the last published rate, and 1-Nov-2026 is a Sunday so it needs the last October rate.
questions.schema:
FX_RATE(rate_date DATE, ccy CHAR(3), rate NUMBER(10,4))
-- one row per business day per currency, no time part
-- rate = INR per 1 unit of ccy
questions.task: Return every calendar day of November 2026 with the USD/INR rate to use and whether it was published that day or carried forward.
questions.hint: Generate a calendar, outer join the rates, include some October rows for the lookback, and use LAST_VALUE(... IGNORE NULLS).
questions.solution:
WITH cal AS (
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-01' + LEVEL - 1 AS d
  FROM   dual
  CONNECT BY LEVEL <= DATE '2026-12-01' - DATE '2026-11-01'
),
src AS (
  SELECT rate_date, rate
  FROM   fx_rate
  WHERE  ccy = 'USD'
  AND    rate_date >= DATE '2026-10-01'
  AND    rate_date <  DATE '2026-12-01'
),
all_days AS (
  SELECT c.d, s.rate
  FROM   cal c LEFT JOIN src s ON s.rate_date = c.d
  UNION ALL
  SELECT rate_date, rate FROM src WHERE rate_date < DATE '2026-11-01'
)
SELECT rate_date, usd_inr, rate_src
FROM (
  SELECT d AS rate_date,
         LAST_VALUE(rate IGNORE NULLS)
           OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS usd_inr,
         CASE WHEN rate IS NULL THEN 'Carried' ELSE 'Published' END AS rate_src
  FROM   all_days
)
WHERE  rate_date >= DATE '2026-11-01'
ORDER  BY rate_date;
questions.why: The calendar guarantees one row per day, and the outer join leaves rate NULL on non-business days. LAST_VALUE with IGNORE NULLS over all rows up to the current one picks the most recent non-NULL rate, and the October rows are only there so 1-Nov has something to look back to. The filter to November is applied outside the window, otherwise the October rows would be removed before the analytic function sees them.
questions.tip: For carry-forward I use LAST_VALUE IGNORE NULLS with an explicit ROWS frame, and I filter after the window so the lookback rows are still visible to it.
questions.simple: On holidays there is no new exchange rate, so you use the last one you had, like a scoreboard that keeps showing the last score until a new goal is scored. LAST_VALUE IGNORE NULLS looks back and picks the most recent rate that is not empty.
questions.remember: IGNORE NULLS = carry the last known value forward.

questions.title: Card EMI due dates in March
questions.scenario: Kavya Nair in credit card operations found that customers who converted a 30-Jan purchase into EMI were billed on 31-Mar, because the old job did ADD_MONTHS on the previous due date. The rule is: due on the same day number as the purchase, or the month's last day if that day does not exist. Purchase timestamps include the time of swipe.
questions.schema:
CARD_EMI(emi_plan_id NUMBER, card_ref VARCHAR2(20), purchase_dt DATE, amount NUMBER(12,2), tenure_months NUMBER, emi_amt NUMBER(12,2))
-- purchase_dt has a time part, e.g. 30-Jan-2026 21:14
-- instalment n is due n months after purchase; tenure up to 60
questions.task: List emi_plan_id, instalment number, due date and EMI amount for every instalment falling due in March 2026.
questions.hint: ADD_MONTHS jumps to the last day of the target month when the start date is a month end (28-Feb becomes 31-Mar), so build the date from the first of the month plus the day number and cap it with LAST_DAY.
questions.solution:
WITH n AS (
  SELECT LEVEL AS inst_no FROM dual CONNECT BY LEVEL <= 60
)
SELECT emi_plan_id, inst_no, due_date, emi_amt
FROM (
  SELECT e.emi_plan_id, n.inst_no, e.emi_amt,
         LEAST(ADD_MONTHS(TRUNC(e.purchase_dt, 'MM'), n.inst_no)
                 + EXTRACT(DAY FROM e.purchase_dt) - 1,
               LAST_DAY(ADD_MONTHS(TRUNC(e.purchase_dt, 'MM'), n.inst_no))) AS due_date
  FROM   card_emi e
  JOIN   n ON n.inst_no <= e.tenure_months
)
WHERE  due_date >= DATE '2026-03-01'
AND    due_date <  DATE '2026-04-01'
ORDER  BY due_date, emi_plan_id;
questions.why: Chaining ADD_MONTHS loses the original day (30-Jan to 28-Feb to 31-Mar), and even a single ADD_MONTHS turns 28-Feb into 31-Mar because of Oracle's last-day rule. Starting from the first of the month, adding the day number minus one and capping with LAST_DAY gives 28-Feb, 30-Mar and 28-Mar exactly as the rule says. TRUNC removes the swipe time and the half-open range from 1-Mar to before 1-Apr catches the whole of 31-Mar.
questions.tip: I always compute instalment dates from the original start date, never the previous due date, and I remember ADD_MONTHS maps a month-end to a month-end.
questions.simple: A due date on the 30th is tricky because February has only 28 days. Start from the 1st of the month, move to the right day, and if the month is shorter, stop at its last day. Always count from the original date, not from last month's date, or the day keeps slipping.
questions.remember: Start from the 1st, add the day, cap at the month's last day.

questions.title: UPI payments from unrecognised devices
questions.scenario: Arjun Malhotra on the fraud desk wants yesterday's high-value UPI payments made from a device other than the customer's bound device. His first query used t.device_id <> d.reg_device_id and missed the riskiest cases: payments where the app failed to capture the device and customers who never bound one.
questions.schema:
UPI_TXN(txn_id NUMBER, cust_id NUMBER, device_id VARCHAR2(64), amount NUMBER(12,2), txn_ts DATE)
-- device_id NULL when the SDK failed to capture it; txn_ts has a time part
CUSTOMER_DEVICE(cust_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, reg_device_id VARCHAR2(64))
-- reg_device_id NULL, or no row at all, if the customer never bound a device
questions.task: List UPI payments of INR 10,000 or more on 11-Nov-2026 where the device does not match the bound device, treating a NULL or missing value on either side as a mismatch.
questions.hint: A comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, not TRUE, so use an outer join and LNNVL (or explicit IS NULL checks) to keep those rows.
questions.solution:
SELECT t.txn_id, t.cust_id, t.amount, t.txn_ts,
       t.device_id, d.reg_device_id
FROM   upi_txn t
LEFT   JOIN customer_device d ON d.cust_id = t.cust_id
WHERE  t.txn_ts >= DATE '2026-11-11'
AND    t.txn_ts <  DATE '2026-11-12'
AND    t.amount >= 10000
AND    LNNVL(t.device_id = d.reg_device_id)
ORDER  BY t.amount DESC;
questions.why: t.device_id <> d.reg_device_id is UNKNOWN when either side is NULL, and WHERE drops UNKNOWN rows, so the riskiest payments vanished. LNNVL(condition) returns TRUE when the condition is FALSE or UNKNOWN, which is exactly 'not a confirmed match'; the LEFT JOIN keeps customers with no CUSTOMER_DEVICE row. The equivalent long form is t.device_id IS NULL OR d.reg_device_id IS NULL OR t.device_id <> d.reg_device_id.
questions.tip: Whenever I write <> on nullable columns I ask what NULL should mean, and for 'not a confirmed match' I use LNNVL or explicit IS NULL checks.
questions.simple: If you do not know which phone a person registered, you cannot say the payment came from the right phone. Oracle treats 'not equal' with an unknown value as 'I don't know' and hides those rows. LNNVL says 'show me anything that is not a sure match', so the risky unknown ones stay in the list.
questions.remember: Unknown is not a match; LNNVL keeps the unknowns.

lessons.why: LAST_VALUE silently returns the current row's value unless you widen the window, a common bug in month-end and closing-rate reports.
lessons.explain: When an analytic function has ORDER BY but no frame, Oracle uses RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. For SUM that gives a running total, but for LAST_VALUE it means the last row seen so far is the current row, so you get the row's own value back. To get the true last value of the partition, state ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, or use FIRST_VALUE with ORDER BY ... DESC. Adding IGNORE NULLS turns it into a carry-forward tool.
lessons.example:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-02' d, 83.10 rate FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-03', 83.25 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-04', 83.18 FROM dual
)
SELECT d, rate,
       LAST_VALUE(rate) OVER (ORDER BY d) AS default_frame,
       LAST_VALUE(rate) OVER (ORDER BY d
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS closing_rate
FROM r;
-- default_frame: 83.10, 83.25, 83.18   closing_rate: 83.18, 83.18, 83.18
lessons.gotcha: LAST_VALUE(x) OVER (ORDER BY d) looks right in a quick test but just echoes x on every row.
lessons.line: For a closing value per period I use LAST_VALUE with an explicit UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING frame, or FIRST_VALUE ordered descending, because the default frame stops at the current row.
lessons.simple: LAST_VALUE sounds like 'give me the last one', but by default it only looks from the top down to the current row, so the last one it sees is itself. To see the real last row, tell it to look all the way to the end.
lessons.remember: Tell LAST_VALUE to look to the end: UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.
